study.title: Psalm 35 Prayer for defense, justice and praise
study.overview: Psalm 35 is an intense supplication of David, in which he asks the Lord to intervene against unjust adversaries, defend him in judgment, and the free from public humiliation. The psalm combines the language of conflict, denunciation of falsehood, memory of David's own integrity and confidence that God will do justice. At the same time that it exposes the wickedness of enemies, the text ends in adoration: the final response of the servant of God is not personal vengeance, but praise to divine justice.

outline.title: Clarment that the Lord may fight for his servant
outline.explanation: David asks the Lord to take on his cause as a defender and warrior. He wants real deliverance, not just inner comfort, and supplicates that God declares his salvation before the threat of persecutors.

outline.title: Request for confusion for the oppressors and joy for salvation
outline.explanation: David asks that the evil plans should fail and the persecutors be frustrated. In contrast to their fall, their soul will rejoice in the Lord, because no one compares to the God who saves the weak from the strongest.

outline.title: Denunciation of injustice and memory of one's fidelity
outline.explanation: The psalmist accuses false witnesses, ingratitude and cruel mockery. He recalls that he treated others with compassion, but received hostility; then he cries out for ransom and promises to praise God publicly when he is saved.

outline.title: End appeal for justice and conclusion in praise
outline.explanation: David insists that his cause is seen by God, asks for a righteous judgment and the shame of those who rejoice with his evil. The psalm ends with the hope that those who love justice will rejoice, while their tongue will proclaim the Lord's righteousness throughout the day.

study.context: The heading attributes the psalm to David. The notes provided accurately relate him to the period of persecution of Saul and his circle, although this is presented as an interpretation and not as absolutely explicit data in the text itself. The Psalm has an individual way of lament with elements of prayer for vindication, judicial denunciation and community praise.
study.theology: The chapter presents God as a just Judge, defender of the innocent and protector of the poor and needy. Justice here is not uncontrolled personal vengeance, but surrender of the cause to the Lord, who sees falsehood, reverses oppression and saves his servant. The moral tension between unjust suffering and faithfulness also appears: David does not deny pain, but turns it into prayer. Moreover, psalm teaches that the proper response to divine intervention is public gratitude and constant praise. For an evangelical Christian reading, the text also echoes the principle that persecuted and hated innocence finds resonance in the experience of Christ, without erasing the original sense of the psalm in its distress situation.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm is a lamentation in which the afflicted servant of the Lord cries out so that God sees his situation and avenges him.
David accuses his enemies of two very grievous evils: false testimony and ingratitude, used to justify his appeal to God.
In conclusion, David declares that his tongue will speak of the righteousness of God, and that this requires constant gratitude for all life.

questions: When I am wronged, do I seek first the defense of God or my own vengeance?
I can remind you, like David, that God sees the lie, manipulation and cruelty, even when they seem to win?
Is my reaction to God's deliverance only personal relief, or also public and persevering praise?
study.practice: Take to God, in specific prayer, a situation in which you feel accused, misinterpreted, or treated with injustice. Instead of feeding bitterness, ask the Lord to judge with righteousness, protect his integrity and turn his answer into a witness. He also practice a concrete form of compassion with someone who has treated him badly, remembering that the psalm does not authorize personal revenge, but trust in divine justice.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text and notes suggest, but they do not prove it absolutely, the historical context of persecution linked to Saul and his allies. There are also poetic elements of imprecity that should be read as a language of prayer for justice, not as authorization for personal aggression. The references of the commentators were summarized without reproducing their original formulations.
